text: Reading Six · Collins, Lo, Park & Haughney (2018) Response Prompting as an ABA-Based Instructional Approach Two teachers with the same question 1 Ms. Creasy, a special education teacher, wants to teach listening comprehension to high school students with severe disabilities who use alternative or augmentative communication (AAC) devices. She hopes her instruction will help students participate in a large-group lesson focused on reading and comprehending literature, and wonders about the most effective instructional strategy. 2 Mr. Jin has peer tutors assigned to work with high school students with moderate intellectual disability. The peer tutors attend a physical education class with the students, and Mr. Jin wonders if there is a simple but effective strategy he can teach them to use during the class. It would be wonderful if all instruction could be errorless. Students who seldom make errors receive more positive feedback from instructors — "You did a great job! I am so proud of you!" rather than "I'm sorry, but that is not the correct answer." Further, praise and other reinforcers increase the likelihood that a student will make the correct response in the future (Cooper, Heron, & Heward, 2007). On the other hand, students who make more errors are likely to practice their errors, allowing them to become ingrained (Collins, 2012). Using systematic instruction based on the provision of prompts is one way to increase correct responses while decreasing incorrect responses. Response-prompting procedures are a specific type of systematic instruction that reflects the principles of applied behavior analysis. Response-prompting instruction All response-prompting procedures are based on conducting instructional trials, which consist of an attentional cue, an instructional stimulus (task direction), a response, and a consequence. Attentional cue.  Can be general ("Let's begin instruction") or specific ("If you are ready to learn, put your hand in the air"), and draws the student's attention to the instructor or the materials. This requires an attentional response that can be general (eye contact) or specific (hand in the air) and indicates the student's attention has been secured. Instructional stimulus.  A task direction that evokes a specific response; it may be verbal, signed, written, or pictorial. Controlling prompt.  To ensure that a student performs a correct response, the instructor inserts a controlling prompt between the stimulus and the student's response — the amount of assistance that a student needs to perform a correct response and receive a positive consequence. Controlling prompts are individualized for each student and each type of task: students who cannot follow a verbal direction ("Enter the number 5 in the calculator") may require a model prompt, and students who cannot imitate a model may require a physical prompt. Prompts are faded from instruction when the student has learned the correct response. Consequence.  Each student response should be followed by an appropriate consequence — reinforcers such as praise, a fist bump, or a smiley face for correct responses; corrective feedback, such as stating the correct verbal response or modeling the correct step, for incorrect responses. Prompting can facilitate appropriate behavior by increasing the pace of instruction, which is more likely to maintain a student's attention and reduce frustration when a student does not know how to respond (Collins, 2012; Wolery & Schuster, 1997). Six response-prompting procedures Researchers have identified six specific and distinct response-prompting procedures for teaching both academic and functional skills: graduated guidance, most-to-least prompting, system of least prompts, progressive time delay, constant time delay, and simultaneous prompting. There is a large supporting research base showing that each procedure works for teaching various content, from single-step discrete skills to multistep chained tasks, with students of various abilities from preschool through adulthood, across settings (school, community, home) and instructors (special or general educators, paraprofessionals, peers without disabilities, family members, related service personnel). Procedure Description Implementation steps Data collection and graphing Graduated guidance (Wolery, Ault, & Doyle, 1992) Uses various levels of physical guidance as needed on a moment-to-moment basis Secure learner's attention and deliver task direction Shadow learner's movements If the learner fails to respond or begins to make an error, immediately use the amount of physical guidance needed to make a correct response Praise prompted as well as unprompted responses Continue until the learner can perform the correct response independently Record independent and prompted responses; graph number or percentage of independent correct responses Most-to-least prompting (Demchak, 1989) Uses a most-to-least intrusive prompt hierarchy across sessions (e.g., physical, model, verbal, independent) Secure attention and deliver task direction Immediately use the most intrusive prompt necessary for a correct response, praising all correct responses After several sessions, move to the next-less-intrusive prompt level Repeat step 3 Continue until the learner responds independently across several sessions Record correct responses at each prompt level; graph number or percentage of correct responses at each level System of least prompts (Doyle, Wolery, Ault, & Gast, 1988) Uses a least-to-most intrusive prompt hierarchy within sessions (e.g., independent, verbal, model, physical) Secure attention and deliver task direction Wait a preset number of seconds (e.g., 3) for the learner to respond independently If the learner responds correctly, give praise; if no response or an error, provide the least intrusive prompt in the hierarchy and wait a set number of seconds If no response or error, repeat step 3 at the next level Continue until the learner responds independently across several sessions Record prompt level needed for a correct response; graph number or percentage of correct independent responses (prompted responses may also be graphed) Time delay, progressive or constant (Walker, 2008) Uses a single controlling prompt delivered after a preset interval that increases progressively across sessions (progressive) or remains constant across sessions (constant) Secure attention and deliver task direction Immediately prompt the correct response (0-second delay) during the first session Deliver the controlling prompt Wait the predetermined response interval (e.g., 3 seconds) Praise correct responses; repeat the prompt for incorrect responses or failures to respond Progressive:  in subsequent sessions, progressively increase the number of seconds before delivering the controlling prompt (1 second in the second session, 2 in the third, 3 thereafter) Constant:  in subsequent sessions, deliver the controlling prompt at a constant interval (e.g., 3 seconds) Record five types of responses: correct before prompt, correct after prompt, incorrect before prompt, incorrect after prompt, no response after prompt. Graph number or percentage of correct responses before the prompt Simultaneous prompting (Morse & Schuster, 2004) Uses daily probe trials to assess student learning, followed by daily training trials using a single controlling prompt delivered after a 0-second delay interval Conduct daily probe trials: secure attention and deliver the task direction; wait a predetermined interval (e.g., 3 seconds); do not prompt responses or correct errors Following probe trials, conduct daily training trials: secure attention and deliver the task direction; immediately deliver the controlling prompt (0-second delay); praise all correct responses or correct all errors Continue daily training trials until criterion is met during daily probe trials Record correct responses during probe trials only; graph daily probe trial data on correct responses only How they differ.  Graduated guidance typically uses physical guidance: the instructor makes a moment-by-moment decision on how much guidance a student needs, shadowing the student's movements and providing assistance only as needed, or systematically fading the amount of physical guidance over time — beginning with hand-over-hand assistance for a student first learning to use a pencil, and fading to just a slight nudge to the wrist. Most-to-least prompting and system of least prompts are more systematic than graduated guidance and rely on a hierarchy of at least three prompts. In most-to-least prompting, the instructor begins with the most assistance in the initial session and systematically decreases assistance across sessions until a criterion of correct independent responses is reached; a student may take several weeks to move through the hierarchy. In the system of least prompts, the instructor begins each trial by allowing the student the opportunity to respond independently before systematically providing increasing assistance. The system of least prompts is especially suited to chained tasks — multistep tasks such as solving a complex equation or preparing a recipe — as it allows the student to complete known steps independently but wait for the amount of assistance needed on the remaining steps. Instead of providing a hierarchy, the time delay and simultaneous prompting procedures rely on a single controlling prompt that will result in a correct response. During the initial session of time delay, the instructor assumes the student needs assistance and immediately provides the controlling prompt following the task direction — a 0-second delay trial. After a preset number of 0-second delay sessions, the instructor begins to increase the delay interval. With progressive time delay, the interval increases by one second at a time across sessions until reaching a predetermined interval (e.g., 5 seconds); with constant time delay, 0-second sessions are followed immediately by a constant interval (e.g., 5 seconds) across all subsequent sessions. In both, correct responses before or after the prompt are always praised; incorrect responses before the prompt are followed by a reminder to wait for a prompt; incorrect responses or failures to respond after the prompt are followed by corrective feedback ("No, the correct answer is rectangle"). The controlling prompt is naturally faded when the student reaches criterion of a set number of sessions of correct responses before the prompt. The progressive time delay procedure may be most appropriate for students who do not know how to wait for a prompt, while the constant time delay procedure may be easier for instructors to implement, as it is not necessary to remember which delay interval is being used. With simultaneous prompting, the instructor always begins with probe trials to determine if the student has mastered the content; if not, daily 0-second delay training trials follow, and the sequence continues until the student meets criterion (e.g., three sessions of 100% correct independent responses) during daily probe trials. Implementing response-prompting procedures efficiently Response-prompting strategies often require less instructional time than other procedures because instructors do not have to spend a lot of time correcting errors. There may be reasons to use a hierarchy of prompts — some students may know how to make a correct response on specific steps of a chained task but need various levels of assistance on other steps, and an instructor using the system of least prompts provides prompts only as needed. Procedures that use a single controlling prompt, however, are typically more efficient because they take less time to implement (Ault, Wolery, Gast, Doyle, & Eizenstat, 1988). Another way to make these procedures more efficient is to add content not directly targeted for instruction — nontargeted information — to instructional trials, and to use strategies that facilitate generalization. Teachers may increase the amount of content a student learns by adding nontargeted information as instructive feedback during trials (Werts, Wolery, Holcombe, & Gast, 1995). For example, the instructor can state related nontargeted information when praising a response: "That is correct — this shape is a square. S-Q-U-A-R-E. A square has four equal sides and four 90-degree angles." Another way is through observational learning, where each student taught in a group has the opportunity to observe the content being taught to other members of the group (Campbell & Mechling, 2009). The instructor can also increase the likelihood that a student will generalize a learned response across settings, people, and materials, as first described by Stokes and Baer (1977) — facilitating generalization of shape recognition (a) across materials by presenting multiple examples (square boxes, square windows, square picture frames, square books), (b) across settings by pointing out square objects as they appear naturally in various school settings, and (c) across people by varying instructors. The goal is for a student to use a new skill with any material in any environment with any person, so it is important to periodically assess generalization across novel materials, settings and persons both while instruction is occurring and when students reach criterion (Cooper et al., 2007). Countering myths Despite the reasons to use response-prompting procedures, there are a number of myths teachers may believe that can decrease their willingness to teach in this way. Myth: it takes a trained special education teacher, in a special education classroom, in a massed trial format, teaching discrete skills one-to-one.  In reality, response-prompting procedures are more flexible and less regimented than teachers may believe — the research shows them used by teachers, peers, paraprofessionals and family members across school, home and community settings, in one-to-one and small-group formats, for discrete and chained skills. Myth: students become dependent on prompts.  There are strategies to decrease this likelihood, such as fading prompts and providing more specific praise or individualized reinforcement (e.g., time to engage in a preferred activity) for unprompted responses than for prompted responses — that is, differential reinforcement. Two lesson plans Lesson plan 1 — Listening comprehension (system of least prompts) Core content standards.  Literacy, speaking and listening: students will read and comprehend literature. Behavioral objective.  After listening to a read-aloud passage, each participant will correctly respond to 5 of 5 WH-comprehension questions by independently pointing to the correct response option on a response board for 3 out of 3 sessions. Instructional context.  Instruction occurs in a group format during a regularly scheduled social studies lesson following an adapted informational text read-aloud. Target students Brett, Quinn and Rhys are each seated in groups with three or four other peers, one of whom is a peer (or paraprofessional) trained to support their learning and AAC turn-taking. Instructional materials.  Data sheet and pen; adapted social studies text; response boards with at least four picture-supported response options (always including at least one "near" example from the same text); and a WH question anchor chart including the word, symbol, basic definition and example of Who, What, When, Where and Why. Procedure — 5 trials per session. Attentional cue:  "Ready to answer questions about the story we read?" Gain the target student's attention with a verbal directive ("Quinn, look at me") and a gesture. Task direction:  individually ask a WH question relevant to the lesson. Correct:  independent response within 3 seconds. Prompt level 1:  if no correct response within 3 seconds, the communication partner rereads the relevant sentence from the adapted text (verbal prompt). Prompt level 2:  if still no correct response, the partner references the WH question chart to remind the student about the type of question being asked and then rereads the relevant sentence (verbal prompt plus explanation). Prompt level 3:  the partner models referencing the WH chart ("A Who question…") and then rereads the relevant sentence (verbal prompt plus model). Prompt level 4:  the partner physically guides the student in identifying the correct answer on the communication device (verbal prompt plus physical guidance). Consequence:  praise the correct response whether independent or prompted ("Great job answering the question!"). Data collection:  the paraprofessional or peer circles the most intrusive prompt level (P1–P4) needed for a correct response on questions 1–5. Maintenance:  once criterion has been met for one day, praise for correct responses is delivered intermittently for two additional days; listening comprehension is monitored at 1-week intervals for 1 month. Generalization:  all students are exposed to multiple exemplars of adapted texts during social studies lessons; Brett is assessed on listening comprehension in other inclusive classes. Behavior management:  all students are intermittently praised for remaining on task; Rhys receives regular praise for staying in his seat or standing area while answering questions. Variations:  listening comprehension instruction can be implemented across subjects from science and literacy to job training; a preference question ("Why did you like this topic?") may be added to connect to personal experiences. Lesson plan 2 — Health core content (simultaneous prompting) Core content standards.  Health: students will summarize the benefits and examples of regular physical activity. Behavioral objective.  When asked two targeted health questions 5 times each, Barbara will respond correctly 10 out of 10 times for 3 days: "Why is aerobic exercise important?" ("Aerobic exercise can make your body healthy and fit.") and "Why is stretching important?" ("Stretching can improve the range of motion of your body.") Instructional context.  Daily probe trials are conducted one-to-one by the special education teacher each day in the resource room, followed by daily training trials conducted by a peer tutor one-to-one in the school gym while walking laps at the beginning of each physical education class. Probe trials (teacher).  Attentional cue — "Are you ready? Look at me," or state Barbara's name. Task direction — alternate asking each targeted question five times each. Consequence — verbal praise for correct responses within 3 seconds; ignore incorrect responses or failures to respond. The same is then done for the nontargeted questions. Training trials (peer tutor).  Attentional cue; ask the first question; immediately state the correct answer and ask Barbara to repeat it; deliver verbal praise or error correction; state nontargeted information ("Walking is a good example of aerobic exercise"). Repeat for the second question, with modelled nontargeted information (upper body stretching postures). Repeat the procedure for 5 trials, alternating between questions. Data collection.  The teacher circles a plus sign for correct responses, a minus for incorrect, and a zero for no response; only data on targeted information counts toward criterion. If a student does not reach criterion on nontargeted information, this is targeted for direct instruction in the future. Maintenance, generalization and behavior management.  Once Barbara meets criterion of 100% correct on targeted content for one day, the teacher fades praise (after every two or three correct responses) for two days; after two weeks, Barbara is reassessed with the same questions. Generalization is assessed by having peers and parents ask the same questions across settings. The peer tutor and teacher periodically praise Barbara for paying attention. Four guidelines for use Select a procedure that is the best fit for the student and the task.  Procedures that initially use more intrusive prompts and provide less opportunity for independence (graduated guidance, most-to-least prompting) may be better suited to young children or students with more significant disabilities, as students are not required to wait for a prompt, be imitative, or know how to follow directions. Procedures that use a single controlling prompt (time delay, simultaneous prompting) may be faster paced and result in less frustration for students with short attention spans. Time delay or simultaneous prompting may be better for discrete skills like math facts or sight words, whereas the system of least prompts may be better for chained tasks where the student can complete known steps but wait for assistance on unknown steps. If two procedures are equally effective, select the one that is most parsimonious or efficient.  Applying the principle of parsimony (Whaley & Surratt, 1968), instructors should pay attention to what works with each student and which procedure is easiest to implement. If time delay and the system of least prompts are equally effective for a task, the teacher might select time delay because it requires only a single controlling prompt instead of keeping up with an entire hierarchy. Efficiency can be determined by which procedure results in the desired outcome in the smallest number of instructional sessions or with the lowest rate of errors. Let data guide instruction.  Instructors should monitor formative data closely, consistently, and frequently — recorded on data collection sheets as instruction occurs and graphed immediately after daily instruction, so visual analysis quickly shows whether instruction is effective. If there is little to no progress over several sessions, the instructor can "tweak" instruction by using a more motivating reinforcer, changing to a more intrusive prompt, or considering whether the student needs to learn prerequisite skills or be taught a complex skill in more detailed steps or smaller chunks (Collins, 2012). Increase efficiency of instruction when possible.  Efficiency can be increased by adding nontargeted information as instructive feedback, teaching in a small-group format to facilitate observational learning, and using strategies that facilitate generalization. When a student reaches criterion on a task, the instructor should do a quick assessment to see if the student has learned additional, nontargeted information; if so, future instructional time can be devoted to other skills. The instructor should also assess generalization across different and novel materials, settings, or people, and provide additional instruction if the student fails to generalize. Summary Response-prompting procedures are a form of systematic direct instruction based on the principles of ABA. There is a large amount of research to support their effectiveness, and the research base continues to grow. Although earlier professional literature focused more on functional skills taught in special education settings, more current research has included core content taught in inclusive settings. Response-prompting procedures are simple enough for almost anyone to learn and flexible enough to be used in a variety of settings with a variety of skills.
